beats.say: A thief broke into a poor monk's hut, late at night. He searched every corner. There was nothing. Nothing at all.
Then the monk came home and found him. My friend, he said, you came such a long way. You must not go back empty-handed. Take my robe.
The thief grabbed the robe and ran off into the dark. The monk sat down at his door, and looked up at the moon.
Poor fellow, he whispered. I wish I could have given him this beautiful moon. For Osho, this is the real wealth: being, not having. Look up tonight.
Chuang Tzu dreamed he was a butterfly, drifting happily from flower to flower, knowing nothing at all about Chuang Tzu.
Then he woke up, and there he was, an old man on a straw mat. Solid. Unmistakable. Chuang Tzu.
But he could not stop wondering. Was I a man who dreamed he was a butterfly? Or am I a butterfly, dreaming now that I am a man?
While you dream, the dream feels completely real. Osho taught: you are the witness, not the dream. Close your eyes, and look for the one who watches.
A carpenter passed a giant old oak, and did not even look up. Useless wood, he said. Too soft for boats, too twisted for beams.
That night the tree came to him in a dream. The useful trees, it said, are cut down while they are young. Their fruits are torn off, their branches broken.
I made myself useless. That is why I am still alive. That is why I grew so big that a thousand oxen can rest in my shade.
Osho taught: not everything must be useful. Keep one part of you useless. A part that only sings, only watches the sky.
A prince watched his cook, Ding, cutting up an ox. It was like a dance. The knife moved through the meat as if it were following music.
Wonderful skill! said the prince. It is not skill, said the cook. I don't look with my eyes any more. I feel the spaces between the joints, and the knife just follows them.
Other cooks chop at the bone, and need a new knife every month. I have had this one nineteen years, and it is as sharp as the day it was made.
Osho taught: don't force life. Feel for the opening... and move through it.
A young monk was given one job: ring the temple bell every morning. He did it quickly, half asleep, thinking about breakfast.
One day the old master called him. Who rang the bell this morning? I did, said the boy. No, said the master. A sleepwalker rang it. Tomorrow, ring it yourself.
The next morning the boy bowed to the bell. He struck it slowly, with his whole being, and listened until the last sound faded into the hills.
The master smiled. Now that is a bell. Osho taught: be total in whatever you do. Even one breath. Listen to it end.

title: No Water, No Moon
ref: A Zen story · Osho, No Water, No Moon

beats.say: For years the nun Chiyono meditated, and nothing happened. Then one night she was carrying water in an old bucket, with the full moon shining in it.
She walked carefully, watching the moon in the water. Suddenly the bamboo band around the bucket snapped, and the bottom fell out.
The water was gone. The moon in the water was gone. And in that instant, Chiyono was free. No water, no moon.
Your mind holds the reflections of everything. One day the bottom falls out. Osho named a whole book after this moment: No Water, No Moon. Look up.
An old master asked his monks for a poem showing what they had understood. The head monk wrote: The mind is a bright mirror. Clean it every day, and let no dust gather.
A kitchen boy who could not read heard it. He asked someone to write his answer on the wall beside it.
There is no mirror. From the beginning, nothing is. Where can the dust gather? And the master chose the kitchen boy.
Osho taught: you don't have to improve yourself forever. You are not the mirror. You are the space it shines in. Rest there for one breath.
A champion archer showed off his skill to an old master. He split one arrow with another. The old man nodded. Good shooting, he said. Now come with me.
He led him to the edge of a cliff, and stood on a narrow rock above the drop, perfectly relaxed. Now, he said, shoot from here.
The archer stepped to the edge, looked down, and his whole body shook. He fell to the ground, sweating, the bow forgotten.
Your skill is in your hands, said the master. Your fear is in your mind. Osho taught: relax, let go. What are you gripping too tightly today?

title: The Tea Master and the Samurai

beats.say: A gentle tea master was challenged to a duel by a rough samurai. He had never held a sword in his life. By tomorrow morning, he would be dead.
He asked a sword master how to die well. First, serve me tea, said the sword master. So he did, slowly, perfectly, with complete attention.
Face him exactly like that, said the sword master. In the morning the tea master raised his sword, and stood utterly calm, without fear.
The samurai found no fear to attack. He bowed, and walked away. Osho taught that fear always comes from the future. Be here, now.

title: Wash Your Bowl
ref: A Zen story · Osho, Hyakujo: The Everest of Zen

beats.say: A new monk arrived at the monastery, eager for deep teachings. Master, he said, please show me the way.
The master asked: Have you eaten your rice? Yes, said the monk. Then wash your bowl, said the master.
The monk stood there, confused. Then, slowly, he understood. There was no special teaching. Only the bowl in front of him, and his attention.
Osho said: "Any mundane activity can become meditative." A cup, a dish, a step. Do it totally, and the temple is wherever you are.
